English: [1][1]  STORY OF THE BEESTUNG PARSON. Among the old stories which I have obtained from the South of the Island, at Cregneish, the one of the bee-stung parson is of particular interest. It was given me in Manx, and runs thus: —

Manx: Ta mee er chlashtyn skeeal veg mysh saggyrt ren coyrt e vreechyn gys thalear dy cherraghey ad fastyr Jesarn, as ren yn thalear cur e[2] vac thie lhieu moghrey Jydoonee.
English: I have heard a little tale about a parson that sent his pants to a tailor on Saturday evening to get mended, and the tailor sent his son with them on Sunday morning,

Manx: Myr ve er yn raad gys thie yn taggyrt, haink eh er edd shellan, as ghow eh breechyn yn taggyrt dy yeealley ny shellanyn ersooyl.
English: and he came on a bees’ nest and he took the parson’s pants to beat the bees.

Manx: As tra ve er gheddyn yn vill hie eh gys thie yn taggyrt lesh ny breechyn.
English: When he got the honey he went on his way to the parson’s house,

Manx: Ren eh lhiggey shaghey spooileil ny shellanyn, as ve traa da’n saggyrt dy gholl ayns yn keeil, chur eh ny breechyn er ayns siyr, as ghow eh toshiaght dy lhaih ny padjeryn ayns y keeyl as ghow ny shellanyn toshiaght dy chur nyn gahyn ayns e lheeayst, as ghow eh toshiaght dy lheimyragh as dy stampey, as haink eh magh lesh goan nagh row cairagh dy ve loayrit ayns keeyl:—
English: and as he had delayed by robbing the bees’ nest, it was about time for the parson to go to church. So he put on the pants in a hurry, and began to read the prayers in the church, and the bees began to sting his thighs, and he began to jump and stamp, until at last he came out with words that were unlawful to be said in church :—

Manx: Va er ve paart dy shellanyn ayns e vreechyn.
English: Some of the bees had been in the pants.

HOW TO STOP BLOOD! — A CHARM.

Manx: Trooid magh yn Ellan shoh veagh persoonyn (deiney dy-cadjin baghey lesh pishagyn oc oddagh lhiettal roie foalley.
English: Throughout this Island there used to be people (generally men) living with charms at them who could stop the running of blood.

Manx: Ayns Skeeyley Chreest ny Hayrey va dooinney baghey oddagh slaanaghey yn roie foalley ec deiney as beiyn myrgeddin.
English: In Kirk Christ Lezayre there was a man living who could heal the running of blood at men and beasts also.

Manx: Dy beagh muc ny booa lhiggey fuill roieagh yn theay faasechredjuagh dy gheddyn yn “fer-obbee.”
English: If there would be a pig or cow letting blood the superstitious peasantry would run to get the “charmer.” A few years ago

Manx: Shiartanse dy vleantyn er dy henney haghyr roie foalley ayns Laxey my-e-chione ta mee er chee dy insh diu.
English: there happened a running of blood in Laxey, about which I am going to tell you.

Manx: Va boirey eddyr daa phersoon, as va’n derrey yeh er woailley yn jeh elley er y chione lesh cainleyr, huitt y dooinney neealloo, as va’n uill deayrtey ass y lhott.
English: There was trouble between two persons, one had struck the other on the head with a candlestick, the man fell in a swoon, and the blood poured out of his wound.

Manx: Hug ad fys da’n “fer-obbee,” haink eh, as hug eh pishag er y dooinney boght.
English: They sent for the charmer, he came, and he put a charm on the poor man.

Manx: Ren yn uill sthappal! — agh roish my dug eh yn phishag er, hug eh boandeyaanrit er e lhott !
English: The blood stopped !— but before he put the charm on him he put a bandage on his wound.

Manx: Myr yeeagh mee harrish boaley chastal my ayr, honnick mee yn marroo cur lesh ny bioee ersooyl.
English: In English :— As I looked over my father’s castle wall I saw the dead carrying the living away.

Manx: Abbyr : “abb” as ny gleaysh dty chab.

English: It was a kind of puzzle ; you cannot say “abb” without moving your chin.

English: Don’t molest me and I will not molest thee.

Manx: Keayrt dy row hie fer mooinjerey dy chur shillcy er e huyr va baghey ayns paart elley jeh’n Ellan.
English: Once upon a time i manservant went to see his sister who was living in another part of the Island.

Manx: Tra v’eh er roshtyn thie e hayrey va traa jinnairagh ayn, as va brott ec e huyr son jinnair.
English: When he arrived at his sister’s house it was dinner time, aud his sister had broth for dinner.

Manx: Hug ee paart da e braar[5], as choud as v’eh g’ee eh, v’ee gra rish, “Nagh vel shen brott mie Bovee!
English: She gave some to her brother, and all the time he was supping it, she kept saying to him, “Isn't that good broth, Boree[6]?
Notes:
[5] Hug ee paart da e braar] original text gives; [Hug eh paart da e vraar].
[6] Bovee] The English version gives the name as [Boree].

Manx: Cha now brott mie myr shen voish Nancy (e ven) Var-a-mish!”
English: Thou’ll not get broth like that from Nancy (his wife) I’ll warrant.”

Manx: Dagh keayrt v’ee gra shoh, va Bovee freggyrt, “T’eh çheh, t’eh cheh,” as cha n’yiarragh eh dy row hh mie, as eiryn oyr shoh v’ee dy mooar seaghnit.
English: Every time she said this, Boree replied, “It's hot, it’s hot,” and she could not get him to say that it was good, a fact which annoyed her greatly.

Manx: Cha leah as va’n brott eeit ec Bovee, b’eign da goll er y raad dy-valley reesht.
English: As soon as he was done dinner, Boree had to start for home again.

Manx: Tra v’eh ersooyl, hooar ee magh nagh row yn eill currit ‘sy vrott eck.
English: When he had gone, she discovered that she had forgotten to put the meat in the broth.

Manx: “Ochannee,” dooyrt ee, “cha nhyrrys da Bovee gra, “T’eh çheh, t’eh çheh.”
English: “Aw well,” quoth she, “no wonder for Boree to say, “It’s hot, it’s hot.”

Manx: Tra v’eh ersooyl, hooar ee magh nagh row yn eill currit ‘sy vrott eck.

English: [25] MANX FISHING - BOAT NAMES [10]. I have collected a number of old Manx names given by the fishermen to their boats, which are both interesting and instructive. I hope others may add to the list. The names come from the south-east of the Island :—

English: I have whetted my sickle sharp,
Notes: [12] er shleeu] ‘whetted’ / ‘honed’. In the origianl text [shleeuit] — an error as a verb is required here. In the 1904 reprint of Manx Notes and Quieries this was changed to [er leeu], which seems to be a typo [er shleeu].

Manx: Dy ghiarrey yn coonlagh marish yn faiyr,
English: To cut the straw- and the grass,

Manx: Dy laboragh fo chiass yn ghrian,
English: To toil under the heat of the sun,
Sweating as if I was in the sea,

Manx: Dy chart ny bunneeyn fo haiee,
English: That I may get the sheaves under the kiln.

Manx: As paart dy lhie er yn laare-vooiee.
English: And some laid on the threshing floor.

Manx: Tra veagh ad fakin eh, veagh ad jannoo braghtan dy arran corkey as eeym, as ceau magh eh.
English: When they saw him they made a cake of oaten bread and butter and threw it out.

Manx: Ta mee cr clashtyn jeh dooinney ren cheet er unnane jeu er y traie, as ren eh coyrt eh ayns yn cheayn reesht;
English: I have heard of a man that came on one of them on the shore, and put him in the sea again ;

Manx: ny lurg shen, tra veagh sterrym er gerrey, veagh yn pohllinagh çheet dy chur raaue da, as cha row eh goit ayns sterrym, choud as ve gholl gys yn cheayn.
English: after that when there was a storm near, the merman was always coming to inform him, and he was not caught in a storm as long as he went out to sea.

Manx: Ta’n ushag veg ruy ersooyl gys y chrouw,
English: The little brown bird has gone to the bush,

Manx: Ny eayin gys ny moiraghyn roie.
English: The lambs to their mothers now run.

Manx: Ta’n oie er yn aarkey lesh co caslys grouw,
English: The night on the ocean appears gloomy.

Manx: Dy gastey cheet voish y shiar-hwoaie.
English: And quickly comes from the north-east.

Manx: Ta fainagh ny ghreiney ersooyl harrish ’oyr,
English: The chariot of the sun is gone over the edge
To the wide waves of the south-west.

Manx: Ta’n eayst ayns shiar er n’irree ayns gloyr,

Manx: As yn sheear ayns e[13] coamrey glass.

English: [31.] MANX NAMES OF FISH AND SHELL FISH.[15]
Notes:
[15] IoME, Sat, Nov 30, 1901; P: 6
Appended below are the Manx names of the piscatorial family, which will no doubt be of interest to Manx fishermen. As it would be very desirable to make the list as complete a one as possible, criticism and corrections are invited. There are many old Manxmen with whom not a few of these names will be familiar, and there are many points which may require clearing up, so I shall esteem it a pleasure to have the list freely criticised. In some cases, two or more Manx names appear for one fish, in others it is hard to determine their English equivalent, while a great many seem to have no Manx name. Some of these are merely translations of their English equivalents, which I have taken the liberty to make. No doubt, not a few of these have Manx names, so I hope that Manx fishermen will peruse the list, and send in any additions or corrections. A list of animals, birds, insects, etc., will follow in due course. J. J. K.

English: [There seems to be no Manx equivalent for the following :—

They used to, and still call the new Christmas the little Christmas, and the old Christmas, the big Christmas, and most of the houses in Cregneish had a stone bench near the front door, to set tubs and other things on to dry. It was called bink, in Manx, and when the Christmas was very near at hand, they used to say : it is under the bench, that is to say, at the door ; and the big Christmas is at the back of the house 'cooil’, that was — it is near, when we’ll get ale to drink and pie with merry cheer. The people of Cregneish keep old Christmas, for they think it is the right Christmas. Old saying of people at Christmas time:
The little Christmas is under the bench .
The big Christmas at the back of the house,

If you ask me the three things the old Manx worshipped above all things, from an epicurean point of view, I may whisper in your ear :

The Herring Moth  [I have seen a very large moth sometimes come in the house late in the evening, when the weather was fine, and it was called the herring moth. When one was seen going about in the house they said there would be good herring fishing that night.]
tit-mouse [was reckoned to be a very bad thing for cattle]
[The old people, when going out of the house at a late hour used t0 say] The peace of God be with me  :

AN OLD MANX BARD AND SOME TEMPERANCE HYMNS, TRANSLATED BY HIM INTO MANX.[67]
Notes: [67] IoME, Sat, May 02, 1903; P: 8: John Quirk of Carn y Greie: G. W. Wood writes: “I resolved if possible to see the old bard for myself, so accompanied by a ‘Mannmagh dooie,’ who had met him and knew something of the eerie district in which he lived, we, i.e., my wife and I, set out to discover him. After traversing some miles of a steep and rugged mountain road we were directed to the house we sought. It was not, however Carn y Greie. The bard had moved to another abode near by. We were admitted by his wife, now, as she proved to be, his widow, for she told us the object of our search was no more. He had been dead several years. She was pleased to see us, and seemed gratified at our desire to see him. She willingly sought out the old bard’s books and papers to show us and amongst them was his old MS. book of “Manx hymns or songs for the use of temperance meetings, and several pieces of poetry suitable on other occasions. Partly composed originally in Manx and partly translated from the English language, by John Quirk, parish of Patrick.” Such is the title it bears on the cover. It had been kept in a damp place, and but for our timely rescue would soon have been illegible, or, indeed, have perished altogether. After drying it before the fire she generously offered it for my acceptance, of which offer, needless to say, I glady availed myself. The book is now well cared for, and I have had all the pieces it contains carefully copied out. These number 69. Of the original compositions, a few have already been published, the best known of them being perhaps “Yn Jeirkagh meshtyllagh” (“The drunken beggar”). The others are Manx translations of English and American hymns. I have sought for some time to discover the originals of these, because no versified translation that could be made into English could be so satisfactory, and I wished to print them in both Manx and English. I have now succeeded in finding the source of a few in a little hymn book kindly lent me by Dr Julian, author of the “Dictionary of Hymnology.” With the editor’s concurrence I purpose sending these for publication, when perhaps some of your Manx linguists will express their opinion upon the merits of the old bard’s translations. To me the rhythm seems particularly pleasing and faithful to the original version. ... After this brief digression I now give the first of the “Temperance Hymns” to be followed by others as opportunity offers for their insertion in the “Examiner.” G. W. WOOD.”
